title: Mega Staircase
reviewNotes: Three final-move comparisons only, from the pictured seven-piece position after Qxh2 at 146s. Nf7 is actual mate and the unique win-preserving move; independently tested Nf3 and Kxf5 lose. Earlier eight/nine-piece staircase, promotion and queen-sacrifice decisions remain unverified source context. This short pattern lesson does not certify the larger staircase.
transcript: White's brilliant idea is knight to G5, and it seems like white is simply losing because black has two pawns that are about to get a new queen, and there is no way to actually access the black king. But, black does need to be a little bit careful. If it promotes this pawn to a queen, this is actually a blunder because knight to F7 would be a checkmate. But, of course, black is free to promote the G pawn to a queen, and now the knight is going to be pinned to the king. And now that there is no checkmate, black is going to get another queen and be completely winning. But, this is where white plays the incredible, majestic, and beautiful queen to D4. A move that doesn't seem to make a lot of sense. It is a check, but it is also blundering the queen. But, we have to remember that the queen cannot move because this would still be a checkmate. But, so what? Black can just block the check. Not with the bishop because that would lead to a checkmate in just a couple of moves. But, instead, it should block it with a knight. Now, the move still is queen to H4, and this time this forces the king to move to G8, and there is no checkmate. What is white trying to achieve? Well, white goes back to C4, and now gives a check, having shifted just one square from the previous one. Black cannot come out because of this checkmate, but it can, of course, just go back to the corner. Now, white could decide to count his blessings and just take a draw by repetition in this position, but that's not good enough. White doesn't want a draw because white continues with queen to C8. The knight drops back, and now it seems like we are just in the same situation that we were in before, but we are not. Now, the check arrives from C3. The queen is gradually managing to move away from the king. Again, black has to cover with the knight, but now queen to H3 forces pretty much the same sequence, and now the queen reaches B8. If I repeat this whole sequence, you can see how the queen gradually moves further away and further away from the king. But the question is what for? What is white trying to achieve? It is not possible to check this king anymore. But it is. Queen to H2 check is the winning move. An incredible sacrifice, remembering the key idea from the start of the position that we just want to dislodge this queen from the pin of the knight. If you don't take, you're just going to lose your queen on the next move. But after black takes, knight to F7 is a beautiful checkmate. If you love incredible chess, follow me for more.
